introduction: These readings begin before the world: a Word through which the heavens and the earth were made, called a dewdrop, the Water of Life and the Primal Light. Genesis, the Psalms, John’s prologue and the Qur’an’s “Be! and it is” stand close beside that opening, and Laozi and the Vedic hymn to Speech not far off. The readings then follow the Word into a Book that speaks, into verses offered as proof, into rain on the heart and the conquest of hearts without a sword, and into the daily work of reading, reciting and doing. The company is not all agreement. Plato doubts that anything written can answer a question; Paine calls every revelation hearsay to its second hearer; Hume asks what testimony could prove; Machiavelli counts the unarmed prophets among the destroyed; and Amos, Jeremiah and Isaiah know seasons when the word is scarce, refused or unheard.
questions: The readings call the Word a dewdrop, water, light and a sun; Jeremiah calls it a fire and a hammer, and Hebrews a two-edged sword. What does each picture claim, and which fits your own experience of a text that changed you?

Plato’s Socrates says that writing, when questioned, “always gives one unvarying answer”, while the readings speak of a Book through which a Voice is heard. What would have to be true of a reader, or of a book, for the second to hold?

Bahá’u’lláh ranks the revealed verses above every other proof, as the Qur’an does for itself. Set this beside Hume’s rule about testimony and Paine’s remark about hearsay. What kind of evidence is the quality of a text, and who can judge it?

The same verses are “a healing and a mercy” to some and ruin to others; Isaiah is told that the people will hear and not understand. Where do the readings and their companions place the cause of that difference?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá holds that peace is unachievable without the power of the Word of God; Hugo and the founders of UNESCO looked to congresses and to education. What does each expect a word to do that the other does not?

James, the Dhammapada and the Mishnah all set doing above reciting, and Claudius finds that words without thoughts never to heaven go. By what signs, in these readings, would a person know that the Word had taken root and was not merely being repeated?

outside.why: The reading calls the Primal Word a light “through whose effulgence the first stirrings of existence were made plain”. Genesis begins at the same moment: darkness on the deep, a word spoken, and light.
The reading has all created things called into being by the injunction “Be Thou”. John opens his Gospel on the same ground: a Word in the beginning, through which all things were made.
“Thine injunction ‘Be Thou’ hath been enforced … and all created things have been called into being.” The Qur’an states the same command in the same word: He says to a thing only Be, and it is.
The Primal Word “hath been called by all names”: Trumpet, Bugle, Path, Balance. The Vedic poet says of the One what the reading says of the Word: the sages give many titles to what is one.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads creation as “an inscribed book” whose beings are letters that “speak with most eloquent tongue”. The psalmist hears the same speech in the heavens, without language, in every land.

For the reading every created thing is a letter in a book of praise. Wordsworth draws the man for whom a primrose is a primrose and nothing more. Is the book of creation legible to anyone who looks, or only to one already taught to read?

The reading traces all things to a Point “from which all things have appeared and unto which they have all returned”. Laozi counts the same descent from one source to the ten thousand things, though his source does not speak.
“But one Letter of His Word” is enough for the reading. The psalm makes the heavens the work of a word and of “the breath of his mouth”: he spake, and it was done.

The prayer names the Word “whereby Thou didst create Thy heaven and Thy earth”. The rabbis count ten utterances in Genesis and ask why ten, when one would have served. What is added when a creating word is spoken more than once?
The Báb writes that God can “bring about the resurrection of all created things through a word”. Ezekiel is shown it done: he speaks as commanded to the dry bones, breath enters them, and they stand.
“The Word of God can never be confounded with the words of His creatures.” The officers sent to arrest Jesus return without him and give that as their whole reason: never man spake like this man.

The reading sets the Word of God apart from every human word. Paine answers that a revelation is revelation to its first hearer only; to everyone after it is a report, to be weighed like any other. How does a reader of a written page stand to the Word the reading describes?

The Word, says the reading, “became manifest without any syllable or sound” and is above what the senses perceive. Elijah finds the Lord in neither wind, earthquake nor fire, but in a still small voice.

A Word “sanctified from any property or substance” is hard to tell from silence. Laozi begins there: the name that can be named is not the enduring name. Does the reading’s Word escape his rule, or confirm it?
“It delivereth you from darkness and guideth your steps.” The psalmist says the same of the word in the same picture: a lamp to the feet and a light to the path.

Revelation is “the Bread which cometh down from Heaven”, and every other gift serves it. Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, answers the tempter out of Deuteronomy: man lives by every word from the mouth of God.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the Word of God “the everlasting, ever-shining Sun” of the realm of thought and morals. Malachi closes the prophets with the same figure, a Sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings.
“The Perfect Man is the expression of the complete thought of the Creator—the Word of God.” John says it of one man, in the sentence on which Christian teaching about Christ turns.

“Man is the sum of Creation,” says the reading. Hamlet can recite all of that, noble in reason and infinite in faculty, and still find in man only a quintessence of dust. What does the reading’s “Perfect Man” add that Hamlet’s praise lacks?
Under the Daystar of utterance the Scrolls “vibrate with joy and ecstasy and shine forth”. The psalm gives the law the same two effects on its reader: it rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes.
“The beginning and the end pointed to one blessed Word.” In the Apocalypse a voice names itself in those terms, Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending.

The prayer hopes that through the Scriptures all may “give ear unto Thy wondrous Voice”. Socrates doubts that any writing has a voice: question it, and it gives one unvarying answer. What would make a book able to speak, as these readings say a Book does?

Each people, says Bahá’u’lláh, “prided themselves” on their Book. Jesus says as much to those who search the scriptures and think they have life in them, yet will not come to the one the scriptures speak of.
“We have a book … what need, therefore, have we of this man?” The Qur’an has a hard picture for those entrusted with a scripture who do not apply it: the ass carrying books.

Those who told Christ that they could “do without him and follow Moses” had a text for it: nothing is to be added to the word commanded. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá has Christ answer, “The book sufficeth you not.” On what ground can a later word be received by people bound to an earlier one?

The revealed verses are “the abiding testimony, the incontrovertible proof”. The Qur’an makes this argument for itself, to those who asked for portents: is it not enough that the Scripture is read to them?

“Their excellence is unrivaled, their virtue nothing can surpass.” This is the Qur’an’s own challenge, on which the reading’s argument is modelled: let mankind and the jinn together produce the like of it.

The reading ranks the verses above all other proofs, as the sun above the stars. Hume sets a rule for any proof of this kind: the falsehood of the testimony must be more miraculous than the fact. Can the quality of a text be weighed on his scale at all?
Beside the verses, other proofs “are as stars”. The parable of the rich man makes the same ranking: those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead.

Bahá’u’lláh says that He “hath had no intention of establishing any position or distinction for Himself”. Jesus answers those who marvel at his learning in the same way: my doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.

The verses are meant to purify the peoples “from the strife and dissension which religious differences provoke”. Swift’s one sentence is the difficulty: we have just enough religion to make us hate. What would make religion enough for the other thing?

“All the peoples of the world are powerless before the revelation of its verses,” the Báb writes of the Bayán. The Qur’an pictures its own weight: sent down on a mountain, it would have humbled and split it.

The teachings of God “are rain-showers of divine mercy”. Isaiah gives the image its fullest form: as rain comes down and does not return until it has watered the earth, so the word does not return void.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes this verse himself and reads its water as the teachings that “cleanse the human heart”. Churches have read it of baptism; the reading takes water and spirit together as one cleansing.

The reading cites the Qur’an’s “pure water” sent from heaven. Another verse works the likeness out: the valleys flow each according to its measure, the foam passes, and what is of use remains in the earth.

At a single melody of the Bird of Eternity the concourse on high “have been enraptured”. The Qur’an describes what the fairest of statements does to those who hear it: the flesh creeps, then flesh and heart soften.
“The waters of everlasting life which flow through the words of the Lord”: Jesus promises the woman at the well a water that becomes in the one who drinks a well springing up into everlasting life.

The rivers of utterance flow “that the tender herbs of wisdom and understanding may spring forth from the soil of your hearts”. The first psalm plants its reader of the law by rivers of water, in fruit and in leaf.

“Will ye not be thankful?” the reading asks beside its rivers. Jeremiah describes the answer a people can give: they leave the fountain of living waters and hew out cisterns that hold none. Why would anyone prefer the cistern?

The reading describes a flood season, rivers of utterance proceeding from the throne. Amos describes the other season: a famine not of bread but of hearing the words of the Lord, and people running to and fro to find them. What would such a famine look like now?

The prayer speaks of “the life-giving effusions” of a Pen that quicken souls. Byron, in a comic poem and of ordinary ink, notices the same power on a human scale: a small drop falling on a thought makes thousands think.
“The greatest philosophers without this Spirit are powerless.” Paul says he came to Corinth without enticing words of man’s wisdom, so that faith should rest on the power of God.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá holds that without the Holy Spirit the philosophers “can do no good work”. The philosopher he might have in view teaches that we become just by doing just acts, as builders by building. Is goodness breathed in or practised?
One man, hearing the Word from a servant, “in an instant … returned from the lowest depths”. Augustine’s turn came as quickly, from a child’s chant over a wall and the first verse his eye fell on.

The verses “so inflamed the hearts that they flew on wings of longing to the place of sacrifice”. Jeremiah knows that fire from within: a word shut up in his bones that he could not hold back, whatever it cost him.

The discerning are “inebriated with the choice wine of His utterance” and the veils are torn. On the Emmaus road the two disciples say what it was like before they knew who spoke: did not our heart burn within us?
“Every single letter … is endowed with such regenerative power as to enable it to bring into existence a new creation.” Peter writes of being born again by the word of God, an incorruptible seed.
“Its pervasive influence is incalculable.” The Epistle to the Hebrews describes how far the word goes into a person: sharper than any two-edged sword, to the dividing of soul and spirit.
The Word is “the master key” that unlocks the doors of hearts. The Dhammapada sets one word of sense, at which the hearer grows quiet, above a thousand senseless ones.

The reading makes the Word the key to hearts, “which in reality are the doors of heaven”. Confucius ends the Analects with a humbler claim: without knowing the force of words one cannot know men. Is his the same key, used on a lower door?

The Word “hath ever dominated and will continue to dominate the realm of being”. Machiavelli reads history the other way: the armed prophets conquered and the unarmed were destroyed. Which histories does each have in mind?
“A mere fisherman was made the repository of Divine wisdom.” Paul reminds the Corinthians what they were when called: not many wise, not many mighty, the weak chosen to confound the strong.

The reading names the fisherman and the shepherd raised by the Word. The council in Jerusalem sees it happen: Peter and John are unlearned and ignorant men, and bold, and the only explanation is where they had been.
The world is set ablaze by “a Word softer than the morning breeze”. Aesop’s fable is the homely form: the wind cannot strip the traveller’s cloak, and the sun’s warmth does it at once.
The reading’s Word is soft as a breeze and is living water. Jeremiah’s is a fire, and a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces. Are these two words, or one word meeting two kinds of heart?

“This motion hath been generated by the potent energies which the words of the Almighty have released throughout the entire creation.” Shelley asks the wind to do as much with a poet’s words: to be the trumpet of a prophecy to unawakened earth.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to the Mount where “the Burning Bush was unveiled”, and has every attentive ear answer, “Here am I!” These are Moses’ words at the bush, in the account the reading draws on.
“God shall, through it, soon conquer the hearts of all who dwell on earth.” The word to Zerubbabel names the means and rules out the others: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

The reading announces a Word that has “encompassed the world”. Arnold, writing in the same decades, hears the sea of faith withdrawing down the shingles of the world. Were they looking at the same shore?
“By one word the world is agitated, and by another word it is calmed and assured.” Proverbs puts both outcomes in the same place: death and life are in the power of the tongue.

Only the Word of God, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, can gather minds and hearts “beneath the shade of one Tree”. Genesis tells how the peoples came apart, and it was by words too: one language confounded into many. What kind of word undoes Babel?

For ‘Abdu’l-Bahá only “a power above and beyond the powers of nature” can turn hatred into fellowship. UNESCO’s founders located both the war and its remedy in the minds of men, to be reached by education and culture. Do the two differ about the illness or only about the medicine?
“One word, if it proceed from a heart pure and stainless, traineth the world of humanity.” Proverbs prizes the single word too, for its fitness: apples of gold in pictures of silver.

Harmony, says the reading, comes through the Word of God and spreads “among the believers of God, who are firm in the Covenant”. Paul grounds the unity of the church the same way, in one Lord, one faith, one baptism.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá stays away from political conferences, since peace “is unachievable save through the power of the Word of God”. Victor Hugo, opening the Peace Congress of 1849, expects the day from the nations themselves. What would each count as evidence?
“Close your eyes to racial differences, and welcome all with the light of oneness.” Paul says what is no longer to be seen among the baptized: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free.
“He hath but to deliver this clear message”, and the hearer may turn aside or choose the path. The Qur’an gives its Prophet the same limit: thou art but a remembrancer, not a warder over them.
From one heaven of verses the believers drink “the wine of everlasting life, while the ungodly drink a scalding draught”. Paul calls the preachers one savour, of life to some and of death to others.

The reading says the same verses kindle hatred in some who hear them. Isaiah is sent with that outcome announced beforehand: hear indeed, but understand not. Does the Word make the deafness or find it?
Whoever heeds the Call is “reckoned among the most distinguished souls, though he be a carrier of ashes”. James asks his congregation whether God has not chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith.
“Will ye be content with that which is like the vapor in a plain?” Plato’s prisoners are content with less, shadows on a wall, and have never turned their heads.
Soar again, says the reading, and “thou wilt again hear that which the people of understanding have not heard”. Paul promises things that eye has not seen nor ear heard.
The reading makes hearing depend on “the power and the capacity” found within. The boy Samuel is taught the first of it by an old priest: to answer, Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes, here in Pickthall’s English: one revelation, a healing and a mercy to those who believe, and ruin to those who do wrong.
“All the inhabitants of earth are recipients of the bounty of the one phenomenal sun.” Jesus draws the same lesson from the same sun, which rises on the evil and on the good.
“Immerse yourselves in the ocean of My words, that ye may unravel its secrets.” Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it over and turn it over, for all is in it, and grow old over it.
The reading has an ocean of words with pearls in its depths. The Qur’an measures the words of God against the sea itself: as ink it would be used up before they were exhausted.
“Think not that We have revealed unto you a mere code of laws.” Paul makes the distinction the reading leans on: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.

The reading promises that immersion will “unravel” the secrets of the words. Tennyson, of merely human words, says that they half reveal and half conceal the soul within. Is a revealed word different in this, or does it hide as it shows?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá is asked what the Apostles’ speaking in tongues meant and answers: “a spiritual tongue, a tongue that embraces all tongues”. This is the account he is explaining.

The reading speaks of one tongue of inner meanings that embraces all tongues. The Qur’an says that no messenger was sent except with the language of his own folk, to make the message clear. How do the one tongue and the many belong together?
The Word is “a sapling, whose roots have been implanted in the hearts of men”, to be tended. In Jesus’ parable the seed is the same everywhere and the ground decides what becomes of it.
“Thou hast attained unto the divine verses; strive that thou mayest attain unto such deeds.” James asks the same step of his readers: be doers of the word and not hearers only.
The reading moves Ahmad on from having the verses to deeds. The Dhammapada says what reciting without doing amounts to: a cowherd counting the cows of others.

The friends are to collect the revealed utterances “and observe them”, and each word will open a door of knowledge. Joshua is given a like charge for one book: to keep it in his mouth and meditate on it day and night, in order to do it.

Collect every utterance you can, the reading urges. The Preacher, who values the words of the wise as goads, adds a tired warning: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. When does gathering texts stop serving the reader?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises a Sunday school where “the Word of God is recited for the children”. Deuteronomy lays the duty on parents: teach these words diligently to thy children, at home and on the way.
“Everyone must have the utmost regard for the dignity of the Word of God.” Jesus’ saying about what is holy and about pearls guards the same dignity, by restraint in where the word is offered.
On the day of meeting they are to “raise such song and melody” that the city hears. The last psalm calls out every instrument for the same purpose.
“Every word that is uttered for God’s sake is like unto a tree.” This is the Qur’an’s own similitude: a goodly saying is a goodly tree, its root firm, giving its fruit at every season.
Whoever serves the Cause “shall endure through the endurance of God’s Word”. Jesus makes the claim on which such a hope rests: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not.

“The essential thing is the Word of God … Pay no attention whatsoever to anything else, not even to the survival of this servant.” Isaiah draws the same line between flesh, which is grass, and the word that stands for ever.

Bahá’u’lláh’s teachings are, says the reading, “like an engraving on stone, firm and steadfast in hearts”. Shelley’s traveller finds words that really were cut in stone, with the empire they boasted of gone to sand. What keeps an inscription alive?

Each of these prayers asks “by” the Word. Claudius, rising from his knees, states the condition any spoken prayer is under: words without thoughts never to heaven go. What do the prayers here bring with their words?
“By Thy most sweet Voice … make me drink of the choice wine of Thine utterance.” The psalmist tastes the words the same way: sweeter than honey to the mouth.
The prayer begs healing “by the pervasive power of Thy most exalted Word”. Psalm 107 remembers it given: He sent his word, and healed them.
An Ocean “every drop of which proclaimeth Thee to be God”. Blake finds a world in a grain of sand and heaven in a wild flower: the whole legible in its smallest part.
The prayer asks that those dear to God be helped “to glorify Thy word among Thy servants”. The psalmist asks it for himself in the fewest words: open thou my lips.
“Enable me to drink deep of the living waters.” The psalm opens on that thirst, the hart panting for the water brooks and the soul for the living God.
“O ye in mortal graves! The peace of God … rest upon you.” The address assumes what Jesus announces in John: the hour when the dead shall hear the voice, and they that hear shall live.

psalm-by-the-word-heavens.text: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth. He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the Lord: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him. For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast

quran-be-and-it-is.text: But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is.

hebrews-worlds-framed.text: Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear

isaiah-word-stand-for-ever.text: All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever

matthew-not-by-bread-alone.text: It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God

jeremiah-word-like-fire.text: The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the Lord. Is not my word like as a fire? saith the Lord; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces

psalm-sweeter-than-honey.text: How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth

amos-famine-of-hearing.text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord God, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord: And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it

john-words-of-eternal-life.text: From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life

psalm-law-is-perfect.text: The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes

deuteronomy-word-very-nigh.text: For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it

psalm-sent-his-word.text: He sent his word, and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions

peter-born-again-by-the-word.text: Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever

joshua-meditate-day-and-night.text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success

ezekiel-eat-this-roll.text: Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel. So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat that roll. And he said unto me, Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness

timothy-all-scripture.text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works

romans-faith-by-hearing.text: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God

john-search-the-scriptures.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life

luke-heart-burn.text: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures

nehemiah-gave-the-sense.text: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading

acts-understandest-thou.text: And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him

ecclesiastes-many-books.text: The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh

proverbs-power-of-the-tongue.text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof

matthew-every-idle-word.text: But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned

psalm-voice-of-the-lord.text: The voice of the Lord is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth: the Lord is upon many waters. The voice of the Lord is powerful; the voice of the Lord is full of majesty. The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars; yea, the Lord breaketh the cedars of Lebanon

luke-seed-is-the-word.text: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. Those by the way side are they that hear; then cometh the devil, and taketh away the word out of their hearts, lest they should believe and be saved. They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away. And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection. But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience

john-never-man-spake.text: Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him? The officers answered, Never man spake like this man

samuel-speak-lord.text: Therefore Eli said unto Samuel, Go, lie down: and it shall be, if he call thee, that thou shalt say, Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth

quran-upon-a-mountain.text: If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah. Such similitudes coin We for mankind that haply they may reflect.

quran-produce-the-like.text: Say: Verily, though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another.

quran-healing-and-mercy.text: And We reveal of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for believers though it increase the evil-doers in naught save ruin.

quran-fairest-of-statements.text: Allah hath (now) revealed the fairest of statements, a Scripture consistent, (wherein promises of reward are) paired (with threats of punishment), whereat doth creep the flesh of those who fear their Lord, so that their flesh and their hearts soften to Allah's reminder. Such is Allah's guidance, wherewith He guideth whom He will. And him whom Allah sendeth astray, for him there is no guide.

quran-give-ear.text: And when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy.

quran-increase-their-faith.text: They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned, and when His revelations are recited unto them they increase their faith, and who trust in their Lord;

quran-ass-carrying-books.text: The likeness of those who are entrusted with the Law of Moses, yet apply it not, is as the likeness of the ass carrying books. Wretched is the likeness of folk who deny the revelations of Allah. And Allah guideth not wrongdoing folk.

quran-ponder-the-quran.text: Will they not then ponder on the Qur'an? If it had been from other than Allah they would have found therein much incongruity.

quran-sea-were-ink.text: Say: Though the sea became ink for the Words of my Lord, verily the sea would be used up before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even though We brought the like thereof to help.

quran-chant-in-measure.text: Or add (a little) thereto - and chant the Qur'an in measure,

quran-rain-and-foam.text: He sendeth down water from the sky, so that valleys flow according to their measure, and the flood beareth (on its surface) swelling foam - from that which they smelt in the fire in order to make ornaments and tools riseth a foam like unto it - thus Allah coineth (the similitude of) the true and the false. Then, as for the foam, it passeth away as scum upon the banks, while, as for that which is of use to mankind, it remaineth in the earth. Thus Allah coineth the similitudes.

quran-no-doubt-guidance.text: This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).

quran-be-originator.text: The Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decreeth a thing, He saith unto it only: Be! and it is.

shakespeare-words-fly-up.text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: / Words without thoughts never to heaven go
shakespeare-words-fly-up.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

dhammapada-cowherd.text: The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others. The follower of the law, even if he can recite only a small portion (of the law), but, having forsaken passion and hatred and foolishness, possesses true knowledge and serenity of mind, he, caring for nothing in this world or that to come, has indeed a share in the priesthood. Chapter

dhammapada-one-word-of-sense.text: Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet

plato-writing-silent.text: I cannot help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting; for the creations of the painter have the attitude of life, and yet if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence. And the same may be said of speeches. You would imagine that they had intelligence, but if you want to know anything and put a question to one of them, the speaker always gives one unvarying answer
plato-writing-silent.author: Plato

rigveda-vak.text: I breathe a strong breath like the wind and tempest, the while I hold together all existence. Beyond this wide earth and beyond the heavens I have become so mighty in my grandeur

byron-words-are-things.text: But words are things, and a small drop of ink, / Falling like dew, upon a thought, produces / That which makes thousands, perhaps millions, think
byron-words-are-things.author: Lord Byron

augustine-take-up-and-read.text: I heard the voice as of a boy or girl, I know not which, coming from a neighbouring house, chanting, and oft repeating, Take up and read … So, restraining the torrent of my tears, I rose up, interpreting it no other way than as a command to me from Heaven to open the book, and to read the first chapter I should light upon
augustine-take-up-and-read.author: Augustine of Hippo

shakespeare-not-marble.text: Not marble, nor the gilded monuments / Of princes, shall outlive this powerful rhyme; / But you shall shine more bright in these contents / Than unswept stone besmear'd with sluttish time
shakespeare-not-marble.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

milton-good-book.text: as good almost kill a Man as kill a good Book; who kills a Man kills a reasonable creature, Gods Image; but hee who destroyes a good Booke, kills reason it selfe, kills the Image of God, as it were in the eye. Many a man lives a burden to the Earth; but a good Booke is the pretious life-blood of a master spirit, imbalm'd and treasur'd up on purpose to a life beyond life
milton-good-book.author: John Milton

tennyson-words-half-reveal.text: I sometimes hold it half a sin / To put in words the grief I feel; / For words, like Nature, half reveal / And half conceal the Soul within
tennyson-words-half-reveal.author: Alfred Tennyson

analects-force-of-words.text: Without knowing the force of words, it is impossible to know men
analects-force-of-words.author: Confucius

milton-omnific-word.text: Silence, ye troubl'd waves, and thou Deep, peace, / Said then th' Omnific Word, your discord end: / Nor staid, but on the Wings of Cherubim / Uplifted, in Paternal Glorie rode / Farr into Chaos, and the World unborn; / For Chaos heard his voice
milton-omnific-word.author: John Milton

emerson-words-are-actions.text: Words and deeds are quite indifferent modes of the divine energy. Words are also actions, and actions are a kind of words
emerson-words-are-actions.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

avot-ten-utterances.text: With ten utterances the world was created. And what does this teach, for surely it could have been created with one utterance?

avot-turn-it-over.text: Ben Bag Bag said: Turn it over, and [again] turn it over, for all is therein. And look into it; And become gray and old therein; And do not move away from it, for you have no better portion than it

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.

avot-not-study-but-actions.text: Shimon, his son, used to say: all my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing better for a person than silence. Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.
